lessons.title: Study Session 1: The Contract No One Signs

blocks.text: Introduction

Amina Yusuf did not read anything in her employment letter about answering calls after work hours, yet within her first month at a logistics firm in Kano she felt the weight of an expectation nobody had written down. This session teaches you to recognise the unwritten agreements that shape every workplace, so you can meet the reasonable ones with confidence and question the unfair ones without fear.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

e Explain why every workplace runs on unwritten expectations as well as written rules. e Identify the informal norms operating in your own workplace. e Distinguish a reasonable unwritten expectation from an unfair or exploitative one.
e Ask a clarifying question about an unclear expectation without appearing incompetent. 2.0 Main Content
A Letter That Did Not Say Everything

Amina Yusuf joined a logistics firm in Kano as a dispatch coordinator, and her employment letter listed her hours, her salary and her leave entitlement clearly. It said nothing about the unspoken expectation that a coordinator answers a driver's call after hours if a shipment is delayed overnight, or that new staff wait to be invited before speaking first in the Monday planning meeting. Amina learned both the hard way, once by missing a call that mattered and once by an awkward silence after she spoke out of turn.
The Agreement Nobody Signs

In 1989, the organisational psychologist Denise Rousseau published a paper describing what she called the psychological contract, the set of unwritten, often unspoken beliefs both an employee and an employer hold about what each owes the other, running alongside the signed employment contract. Her finding was significant: because this contract is never written down, each side can hold a different, unstated version of it, and real friction usually appears not because someone broke a rule, but because someone broke an expectation the other side did not know she held.
Reading the Unwritten Rules
Watching Before Assuming

The first two or three weeks in any role are usually the richest source of information about a workplace's real norms, who speaks first in a meeting, how quickly messages are expected to be answered, whether lunch is taken together or alone, and watching carefully before assuming a norm from a previous job still applies here saves an avoidable misstep.
Naming a Norm Out Loud When It Is Unclear

An unwritten expectation is often easiest to confirm by naming it plainly to a trusted colleague or supervisor, asking directly whether a pattern she has noticed is in fact expected, rather than guessing and risking a wrong assumption in either direction.
Recognising When an Unwritten Expectation Crosses a Line

Not every unwritten expectation deserves to be met quietly. An expectation that asks her to work consistently unpaid hours, absorb a colleague's duties permanently without acknowledgement, or stay silent about a genuine safety concern has moved from a workplace norm into something worth raising directly, calmly and specifically, with a supervisor or through the channel her workplace provides for it.
Key Practices
e Observe a new workplace's real patterns for the first few weeks before assuming your last job's norms still apply.
e Name an unclear expectation out loud to a trusted colleague or supervisor rather than guessing. e Meet a reasonable unwritten expectation the same way you would meet a written one.
e Recognise and raise an unwritten expectation that has become unfair or exploitative.
A Worked Example: Amina's Two Lessons

The missed after hours call cost the firm a night of confusion over a delayed shipment, and Amina's supervisor was frank with her afterward: dispatch coordinators are expected to stay reachable when a shipment is actively moving, an expectation that had never appeared in writing because everyone before her had simply learned it from a colleague early on.

The Monday meeting was different. When Amina finally asked a trusted colleague why new staff seemed to wait before speaking, she learned it was not a rule at all, simply a habit the previous two coordinators had fallen into out of nervousness, not expectation. Once she understood that, she began contributing from her second month onward, and no one so much as blinked.
Common Pitfalls

New employees often assume that every unwritten pattern they notice is a firm expectation, when some patterns are simply habits other people fell into rather than anything actually required. Treating every observed pattern as arule can make a new employee more anxious and less herself than the workplace actually asks for.
Meeting the Contract Honestly

None of this asks Amina to guess forever. It asks her to watch, ask when something is unclear, and hold the line when an unwritten expectation stops being reasonable, so that the invisible agreement she is actually part of matches the one she believes she signed.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned that every workplace runs on unwritten expectations alongside written rules, and practised reading, confirming and, where necessary, questioning them. This prepares you for Study Session 2, where the same clear-eyed honesty applies to how you manage your own time and reliability.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Name one unwritten expectation you have noticed in your own workplace or community. How did you first learn it?
2. Think of a time you assumed a norm from one setting applied in another, and were wrong. What did you learn from it? Practical Output: Practical Output
A short list of three unwritten expectations noticed in a real workplace, each marked as reasonable, unclear, or
worth raising.
References and Further Reading
e Rousseau, D.M. (1989). Psychological and implied contracts in organizations. Employee Responsibilities and Rights Journal, 2(2), 121 to 139.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Ecclesiastes 9:10, on doing whatever your hand finds to do with all your might.
e Qur'an, Surah At-Tawbah 9:105, on working, for Allah will see your deeds, and His Messenger and the believers.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 2: Showing Up On Time, On Purpose

blocks.text: Introduction

Thandiwe Banda rebuilt her working life in Lilongwe after resettling from a difficult chapter elsewhere, and she knew that being seen as reliable, showing up when she said she would, would matter more to a new employer than any single skill on her CV. This session teaches you to turn a good intention to be on time and dependable into a plan specific enough to actually survive a hard morning.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:
e Explain why reliability is judged by small, repeated actions rather than grand gestures. e Turn a vague intention into a specific, triggered plan.
e Anticipate the situations most likely to derail punctuality.
¢ Build one simple daily habit that protects a commitment.
e Recover credibly from a single lapse without letting it become a pattern. 2.0 Main Content
A Reputation Built in Small Moments

Thandiwe Banda works as a receptionist at a clinic in Lilongwe, and in her first two weeks she was late twice, both times by less than ten minutes, both times for reasons that felt minor to her, a delayed minibus, a slow queue at a shop. Her supervisor's concern was not about either single morning. It was about what a pattern of small lateness would say about her reliability before anyone had the chance to see her actual skill at the desk.
Turning a Wish Into a Plan

In 1999, the psychologist Peter Gollwitzer published a review in American Psychologist showing that people who forma specific, if-then plan, naming exactly when and how they will act, follow through on their goals substantially more often than people who simply intend to do something in general. A general intention to be on time is easy to hold and easy to break. A specific plan, naming the exact minibus she will catch and what she will do if it is late, is far more likely to survive an ordinary difficult morning.
Building a Plan That Survives a Hard Morning

Naming the Trigger, Not Just the Goal A strong plan states exactly what situation will prompt the action, if the 6:40 minibus has not arrived by 6:50, | will start walking toward the next stop, rather than a general resolve to leave early enough.
Planning for the Likely Obstacle, Not Just the Ideal Morning

The single biggest improvement in a punctuality plan usually comes from naming, in advance, the one or two things most likely to go wrong, a late minibus, a queue, a forgotten item, and deciding now what she will do when, not if, one of them happens.
Protecting the Plan With a Small, Repeatable Habit

A habit repeated daily, laying out what she needs the night before, checking the time at one fixed point in her morning routine, removes the plan from depending on willpower alone and makes it far more likely to hold on an ordinary tired morning.
Key Practices

e State your punctuality plan as a specific if-then rule, not a general intention. e Name the one or two obstacles most likely to derail your plan, in advance. e Build one small, repeatable habit that protects the plan without relying on willpower alone. e Treat a single lapse as information to adjust the plan, not evidence that the plan has failed.
¢ Communicate proactively the moment you know you will be late, rather than waiting to be asked.
A Worked Example: Thandiwe's Revised Morning

After her supervisor's conversation, Thandiwe built a specific plan rather than a renewed general resolve. If the 6:40 minibus has not arrived by 6:50, she now walks to the next stop rather than waiting. She lays out her bag and clinic uniform the night before, a habit that takes under five minutes and removes one entire source of morning delay. She also agreed with her supervisor that if she is ever going to be more than five minutes late, she will call the front desk the moment she knows it, rather than arriving apologetic and unannounced.

She has been late once since, a genuinely unusual traffic closure, and she called ahead twenty minutes before her shift began. Her supervisor's response was entirely different from the earlier conversation, because a single, well- communicated exception inside a reliable pattern reads very differently from an unpredictable one.
Common Pitfalls

Treating a single lapse as proof that the whole effort has failed is the error that undoes this stage fastest, leading either to abandoning the plan altogether or to over-apologising in a way that draws more attention to the lapse than the recovery deserves. A reliable person is not someone who never has a difficult morning. She is someone whose difficult mornings are rare, communicated early, and do not repeat.
A Reputation Rebuilt on Purpose

Thandiwe's reliability now rests on a small, specific system rather than a hope that today will go smoothly, and that system, more than any single morning, is what her supervisor and colleagues have actually come to trust.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to turn a general intention to be reliable into a specific, triggered plan built around the obstacles most likely to derail it. This prepares you for Study Session 3, where the same specificity shapes how you communicate at work.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 1. Name one specific if-then plan you could build for a commitment you regularly struggle to keep.
2. Think of the last time you were late or missed a deadline. What single obstacle actually caused it, and how could a plan address it in advance? Practical Output: Practical Output
One written if-then plan for a real, recurring commitment, naming the specific trigger, the planned action, and one backup habit.
References and Further Reading
¢ Gollwitzer, P.M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist, 54(7), 493 to 503.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Ephesians 5:15 to 16, on looking carefully how you walk, making the best use of the time.
¢ Qur'an, Surah Al-Asr 103:1 to 3, on time, and those who believe and do righteous deeds.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 3: Saying It So It Lands

blocks.text: Introduction

Assia Bensalem used to plan her reply while a colleague was still talking, certain she already understood the point being made. This session teaches you to listen for what is actually being said before responding, and to write and speak at work so your own message actually lands the way you intend it to.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

e Distinguish listening to respond from listening to understand. e Write a workplace message that states its purpose in the first line. e Match your tone to the relationship and the stakes of the message.
e Ask a clarifying question instead of guessing at an unclear instruction. 2.0 Main Content
A Meeting Where Nothing Landed

Assia Bensalem coordinates client onboarding for a telecommunications firm in Algiers, and for months her team meetings ran long without actually resolving anything, because everyone, herself included, was mentally preparing a response while a colleague was still speaking, rather than actually taking in what was being said. A new team lead noticed the pattern within a single meeting and named it plainly.
Listening as an Active Skill

In 1957, the psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson published Active Listening through the Industrial Relations Center at the University of Chicago, describing listening not as a passive act of hearing but as an active discipline, attending fully to both the content and the feeling behind what a speaker says before formulating any response. Their central point was direct: most people listen with the intention of replying, not the intention of understanding, and the difference is usually obvious to the person speaking.
Communicating So It Actually Lands

Listening Before Replying Waiting until a colleague has genuinely finished her point, and being able to summarise it accurately before responding, is the clearest sign that listening, not merely waiting for a turn to talk, has actually taken place.
Leading a Message With Its Purpose

Aworkplace message, written or spoken, lands more clearly when its purpose appears in the first line, | need your approval on this by Thursday, rather than being buried at the end of several paragraphs of context the reader has to wade through first.
Matching Tone to the Moment

The same information can be delivered warmly or coldly, briefly or at length, and the right choice depends on the relationship and the stakes involved; a message to a close colleague about a minor delay can be brief and informal, while a message to a client about a serious issue needs more care and completeness.
Key Practices .
e Listen to understand fully before preparing a response. ¢ Confirm you have understood a colleague's point before replying to it. ¢ Open a workplace message with its actual purpose.
e Match your tone to the relationship and the stakes of what you are communicating.
A Worked Example: Assia's Meetings, Before and After

Assia's old habit, in a meeting where a colleague raised a concern about a client's onboarding timeline, was to begin formulating her own response about a different but related issue before the colleague had finished speaking, which meant her reply often addressed a point slightly different from the one actually raised.

Her new habit, practised deliberately over several weeks, is to let the colleague finish completely, and to open her own response with a one sentence summary of what she heard, so | understand the concern is specifically about the client's first week, before adding anything of her own. Meetings on her team now run shorter, not because people say less, but because fewer points need to be repeated a second time to be properly heard.
Common Pitfalls

Confusing volume of talking with quality of communication trips up many beginners, adding more words to a message or a meeting contribution in the belief that this makes a point clearer, when a shorter message with its purpose stated plainly at the start is usually understood faster and more accurately than a longer one.
A Habit Worth the Extra Second

The pause Assia now takes before replying, to actually finish listening rather than preparing her next sentence, costs her almost nothing in time and has changed how often she needs to repeat herself.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to listen actively before responding and to communicate with a clear purpose stated early. This prepares you for Study Session 4, where the same discipline shapes how consistently you follow through on your work.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Think of a recent conversation where you were preparing your response while the other person was still speaking. What did you likely miss?
2. Rewrite one recent workplace message you sent so its purpose appears in the first line. Practical Output: Practical Output
One workplace message rewritten with its purpose in the first line, and a one-paragraph reflection on a conversation improved by listening fully before responding.
References and Further Reading

e Rogers, C.R., & Farson, R.E. (1957). Active Listening. Chicago: Industrial Relations Center, University of Chicago. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Ephesians 4:29, on letting no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only what is good for building up. e Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari 6018, on whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day speaking good or remaining silent. .
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 4: The Work No One Is Watching

blocks.text: Introduction

Nobody was tracking whether Emmanuel Cham refilled the printer paper or double checked a shared file before sending it onward, and that is exactly the point of this session: work ethic is measured most honestly in the tasks no one is watching, not the ones that earn visible credit.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:
¢ Distinguish work ethic from simple compliance.
e Describe what going beyond the minimum actually looks like in a specific role. e Own a mistake without deflecting blame.
e Explain why small acts of integrity build trust over time.
e Recognise the difference between helpfulness and self-neglect. 2.0 Main Content
The Task No One Assigned

Emmanuel Cham works as an administrative assistant at a small import business in Banjul, and for his first few months he did exactly what his job description asked, and nothing more, arriving on time, completing assigned tasks, leaving punctually. When a colleague's shipment paperwork went missing before a deadline, Emmanuel noticed the error while doing something unrelated, and had a choice nobody would have questioned him for making either way: mention it and help fix it, or let it become someone else's problem to discover.
The Behaviour No Job Description Captures

In 1988, the organisational researcher Dennis Organ published Organizational Citizenship Behavior: The Good Soldier Syndrome, describing the voluntary, often invisible actions employees take that go beyond their formal duties, helping a colleague under pressure, protecting a shared resource, catching an error nobody assigned them to catch. His finding was clear: organisations run measurably better when employees engage in this kind of behaviour, even though it rarely appears in a job description or gets directly rewarded.
Practising Work Ethic Where No One Is Watching

Doing the Unassigned Task Anyway Noticing a problem outside her formal responsibility and choosing to flag it or fix it, rather than deciding it is someone else's job, is one of the clearest, most consistent signs of real work ethic.
Owning a Mistake Plainly

Naming her own error directly and specifically, rather than explaining it away or quietly hoping it goes unnoticed, is what actually builds trust after something has gone wrong, because a colleague who owns a mistake plainly is far easier to rely on going forward than one who does not.
Protecting Her Own Limits Honestly

Work ethic is not the same as never saying no. Taking on every extra task without ever naming her own limits eventually produces a worse outcome for everyone, a missed deadline, a rushed job, exhaustion, than honestly naming what she can and cannot take on this week.
Key Practices

e Notice and act on a problem outside your formal responsibility, rather than assuming it is someone else's. e Own a mistake directly and specifically, without deflecting blame. e Treat small, unglamorous tasks with the same care as visible ones. e Name your own limits honestly rather than accepting every request out of guilt.
e Build trust through consistent, small actions rather than occasional grand gestures.
A Worked Example: Emmanuel's Missing Paperwork

Emmanuel flagged the missing shipment paperwork to his colleague immediately, and together they traced it to a filing error made two days earlier, in time to correct it before the deadline. Nobody had assigned him to check that folder that afternoon. He simply noticed something wrong and treated it as worth fixing rather than someone else's problem.

Three weeks later, Emmanuel made his own filing error, misplacing an invoice that delayed a payment by two days. He told his supervisor directly the moment he noticed, before anyone else discovered it, and named exactly what had gone wrong and what he had done to correct it. His supervisor's trust in him did not decrease after that conversation. If anything, it grew, because the way he handled his own mistake matched the way he had handled someone else's weeks earlier.
Common Pitfalls

Treating work ethic as an unlimited obligation to say yes to every request is a mistake that eventually produces burnout and, ironically, worse work rather than better. Real work ethic includes the honesty to say this is more than | can do well by Friday, before a rushed or incomplete result becomes the actual outcome.
What Trust Is Actually Built From

Emmanuel's reputation at the import business was not built on one dramatic moment. It was built from a series of small, unglamorous choices, flagging a problem, owning a mistake, saying no honestly when needed, none of which anyone was watching closely enough to notice individually, but all of which added up to something his colleagues now rely on.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned that real work ethic shows up most clearly in the tasks no one is watching, and that owning a mistake plainly builds more trust than avoiding one quietly. This prepares you for Study Session 5, where that same trust shapes how you receive feedback from others.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Describe one recent situation where you noticed a problem outside your formal responsibility. What did you choose to do, and why?
2. Think of a time you owned a mistake directly. How did the other person respond, and what does that tell you? Practical Output: Practical Output
Awritten account of one recent unassigned task noticed and acted on, and one mistake owned directly, with what each revealed about her own work ethic.
References and Further Reading

e Organ, D.W. (1988). Organizational Citizenship Behavior: The Good Soldier Syndrome. Lexington, MA: Lexington Books. Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Proverbs 11:3, on the integrity of the upright guiding them.
¢ Qur'an, Surah Al-Mutaffifin 83:1 to 3, on woe to those who give less than due in dealing with others.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 5: Taking the Correction Well

blocks.text: Introduction

Consolata Uwase rebuilt her career in Kigali after being widowed, returning to paid work after several years away, and the hardest early moment was not a difficult task but a piece of blunt feedback from a much younger supervisor. This session teaches you to receive feedback as information about your work, not a verdict on your worth, so that a correction becomes something you can actually use.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:
e Distinguish feedback about your work from judgement of your worth.
e Separate a defensive first reaction from a considered response.
e Ask one clarifying question before responding to critical feedback.
e Identify one concrete change to make from a piece of feedback.
e Explain why treating ability as capable of growth changes how feedback is received.
e Track whether a change actually took hold over time. 2.0 Main Content
A Correction That Stung More Than It Should Have

Consolata Uwase returned to paid work in Kigali as a bookkeeper for a small trading company after several years away following her husband's death, and her first piece of direct feedback, that a report she had prepared contained three formatting errors that made it hard to read, left her quietly rattled for the rest of the day. The report was fixable in twenty minutes. Her reaction to the feedback took considerably longer to settle.
Two Ways of Understanding Ability

In 1988, the psychologists Carol Dweck and Ellen Leggett published a study in Psychological Review describing two different ways people implicitly understand their own ability. People who believe ability is fixed tend to experience critical feedback as a threat to their sense of competence and often disengage or become defensive. People who believe ability can be developed through effort tend to experience the same feedback as useful information and respond by trying a new approach. The difference is not how talented either person actually is. It is what each one believes talent can become.
Receiving a Correction Without Losing Herself in It
Separating the First Reaction From the Real Response

The first flash of embarrassment or defensiveness after critical feedback is a normal reaction, not a decision, and giving herself a moment before responding, even a single breath, usually produces a steadier, more useful reply than reacting in that first flash.
Asking One Clarifying Question

Asking a specific question, could you show me exactly where the formatting broke down, turns a vague sting into something concrete and workable, and usually signals to the other person that the feedback landed and was taken seriously.
Naming One Actual Change

Feedback becomes useful the moment it produces one specific, nameable change, reviewing a report against a formatting checklist before sending it, rather than staying as a vague resolve to be more careful in general.
Key Practices

¢ Give yourself a brief pause between hearing feedback and responding to it. e Ask one clarifying question to turn vague feedback into something specific. e Separate what was said about the work from any story you are telling yourself about your worth. e Name one concrete change you will make as a result of the feedback.
e Check back later whether the change actually held.
A Worked Example: Consolata's Report, Revisited

In the hour after the feedback, Consolata's first instinct was to conclude that she had been away from paid work too long and no longer belonged in the role. She recognised the thought as the sting talking, not a fact, and asked her supervisor the next morning to walk through exactly where the formatting had gone wrong, rather than avoiding the subject.

The clarifying conversation revealed something specific and fixable: she had been using a spacing convention from years earlier that the company's current template no longer used. She built herself a one-page checklist from that conversation, and her next four reports came back with no formatting corrections at all. The correction had nothing to do with her competence as a bookkeeper and everything to do with one outdated habit she had never had a reason to update.
Common Pitfalls

Treating a single piece of critical feedback as proof of a much larger, permanent shortcoming is a common misstep at this stage, and it usually produces exactly the disengagement that makes future feedback harder to receive rather than easier. A specific correction about one report is information about that report, not a verdict on a person's entire competence.
What Actually Changed

Consolata's formatting improved within days. What changed more slowly, and mattered more, was how quickly she now separates a correction about her work from any conclusion about her own worth, a shift that has made every piece of feedback since noticeably easier to actually use.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to receive feedback as usable information rather than a judgement of your worth, and to turn a correction into one concrete change. This prepares you for Study Session 6, where every habit from this course comes together in how you present yourself professionally.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Recall a recent piece of feedback that stung. Looking back, was it about your work specifically, or did it feel like a judgement of your worth?
2. Name one concrete change you could make in response to feedback you have received but not yet acted on. Practical Output: Practical Output
Awritten account of one piece of feedback received, the clarifying question asked, and the one concrete change made as a result.
References and Further Reading
e Dweck, C.S., & Leggett, E.L. (1988). A social-cognitive approach to motivation and personality. Psychological Review, 95(2), 256 to 273.
Optional further reading, curriculum-team reviewed: e Proverbs 12:1, on loving discipline and knowledge.
e Hadith, Sunan Ibn Majah 224, on seeking knowledge being an obligation upon every believer. .
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: What the Room Sees First

blocks.text: Introduction

Every session so far has built one habit. This final session asks Joseph Okello, and you, to notice that all of it, punctuality, communication, work ethic, how feedback is received, is also read by the people around you as a single, continuous impression, in the room and on the screen, and to shape that impression on purpose rather than by accident.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this study session, you should be able to:

e Explain why professional presence is shaped deliberately rather than left to chance. e Align how you present yourself with the message you actually intend to send. e Apply the same care to your digital conduct as to an in-person meeting.
¢ Carry the habits from Sessions 1 to 5 into one consistent professional presence. 2.0 Main Content
The Meeting Joseph Almost Slept Through

Joseph Okello works remotely for a regional accounting firm from Kampala, and for his first video call with a new client he joined from his bed, camera angled upward, still in the shirt he had slept in, assuming that because the meeting was virtual, none of it mattered the way an in-person meeting would. The client's tone on that call was polite but noticeably cooler than it became once Joseph corrected course for their second meeting.
A Performance Given Whether We Intend It or Not

In 1959, the sociologist Erving Goffman published The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, describing how people in any social setting, a workplace included, continuously manage the impression they give others, whether or not they mean to be doing so. His central point was that there is no neutral, impression-free way to show up. Every choice, posture, setting, tone, timing, is read as information by the people watching, which means professional presence is either shaped on purpose or left to chance, never actually absent.
Shaping the Impression on Purpose

Aligning Setting and Posture With the Message Aworkspace, lighting and posture that match the seriousness of a meeting, sitting upright at a desk rather than reclining in bed, send the same signal a colleague reads instantly in person: this meeting has my full attention.
Carrying Digital Conduct as Seriously as In-Person Conduct

A message sent late at night, a video call joined without a camera check, a chat reply typed in a tone that would never be used face to face, are all read by a colleague or client as real information about her professionalism, exactly as an in-person habit would be.
Letting the Earlier Habits Show Up Together

Professional presence is not a separate seventh skill. It is what happens when reliability, clear communication, consistent work ethic and openness to feedback are visible together, in the same room or on the same screen, rather than practised one at a time.
Key Practices

e Match your setting, posture and tone to the seriousness of the moment, in person and on screen. ¢ Give digital conduct, messages, calls, timing, the same care as in-person conduct. e Notice what your environment is communicating before a meeting begins, not after.
e Let the habits from earlier sessions show up together, not as separate performances.
A Worked Example: Joseph's Second Meeting

For his second call with the same client, Joseph moved to a small desk near a window, checked his camera angle and lighting beforehand, and wore the same collared shirt he would have chosen for an in-person meeting. He joined two minutes early rather than exactly on time, a small habit carried directly from Session 2.

Nothing about his actual accounting advice changed between the two meetings. The client's warmth did. By the end of the second call, she was asking his opinion on a matter slightly outside the meeting's original agenda, a small but real sign of a trust the first meeting had not yet earned.
Common Pitfalls

Assuming that professional presence is only about appearance is the most common misstep at the capstone stage, when in practice it is the visible sum of every habit this course has built, arriving on time, communicating clearly, following through, receiving correction well. Polishing a camera setup while ignoring reliability or follow-through produces a presence that looks composed briefly and unravels quickly.
One Continuous Impression

Joseph's clients now experience one consistent person across a phone call, a video meeting and a written report, not because he performs differently for each, but because the habits underneath all of them are finally the same habits, practised on purpose.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned that professional presence is shaped deliberately, in person and online, and that it is the visible sum of the habits built across this entire course. This closes Course 66 and prepares you for Course 67, Workplace Communication and Collaboration.
Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment
1. Think of a recent meeting, in person or virtual, where your setting or posture may have sent an unintended message. What would you change?
2. Looking back across all six sessions, which single habit do you most need to carry forward into how you present yourself at work? Practical Output: Practical Output
